issues.legal_issue: A judgment may be reviewed when it overlooks a retrospectively operative amendment that governed the transaction and could change the result.
material_facts: The Court had previously dismissed an appeal on the ground that the sale of standing trees was not a sale of goods chargeable to sales tax.
Before the appeal was decided, a state amendment took retrospective effect to include standing timber agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale.
The amendment was not brought to the Court’s attention when it decided the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The Court reviewed its judgment because the omission of the applicable retrospective amendment was an error apparent on the face of the record.
issues.legal_principle: A judgment that suffers from an error apparent on the face of the record may be reviewed. The Court applied that principle because the overlooked amendment had retrospective operation and governed the transaction at issue.

predicates.review_proceeding: A party asks the court to review a judgment it previously issued.
predicates.retrospective_amendment_applied: An amendment applied retrospectively to the transaction decided in the prior judgment.
predicates.amendment_overlooked: The prior judgment was issued without the court being informed of the applicable amendment.

issues.definition: When a review proceeding concerns a judgment that overlooked an applicable retrospective amendment, the prior judgment is reviewed.

issues.legal_issue: Standing timber attached to land is goods for sales-tax purposes when the sale contract requires it to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale.
material_facts: The sale concerned timber standing on land.
The contract expressly provided that the timber was to be severed under the contract of sale.
A retrospective state amendment included standing timber agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale in the definition of goods.
The dispute arose in an appeal concerning whether the sale was chargeable to sales tax.
issues.conclusion: The timber was goods within the meaning of the Sale of Goods Act, the state amendment was valid as applied to the transaction, and the appeal was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “sale of goods” in Entry 54 of List II has the same meaning as in the Sale of Goods Act, 1930; a State Legislature cannot extend it to transactions that are not sales of goods within that Act. Under section 2(7) of that Act, however, things attached to land are included as goods when the contract provides for their severance before sale or under the contract of sale. The Court relied on The State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co. (Madras) Ltd. and Pandit Banarsi Das Bhanot v. The State of Madhya Pradesh for the meaning of “sale of goods,” and on the inclusive definition in section 2(7) to find the timber covered here.

rule.if: sales_tax_appeal and standing_timber_attached_to_land and contract_requires_severance and state_definition_covers_severable_timber

predicates.sales_tax_appeal: The case is an appeal about whether a transaction is chargeable to sales tax.
predicates.standing_timber_attached_to_land: The subject of the sale is timber that remains standing and attached to land.
predicates.contract_requires_severance: The sale contract provides that the timber is to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale.
predicates.state_definition_covers_severable_timber: A state enactment includes standing timber agreed to be severed before sale or under the contract of sale in its definition of goods.

issues.definition: In a sales-tax appeal, when a state enactment covers severable standing timber and the contract requires severance, the sale is treated as a taxable sale of goods.
